name: Valerian root

lead: Valerian root is an old European herbal remedy sold for sleep and nervous tension. It shows up in bedtime routines in recovery and appearance communities, where better sleep is tied to skin and recovery.

Lab work suggests valerenic acid enhances GABA-A receptor activity. Reviews differ: a 2010 meta-analysis and 2006 review suggested possible benefit, a 2015 review and a 2017 AASM guideline called effectiveness weak or inconclusive, and a 2020 meta-analysis concluded it may be effective, suggesting variable extract quality explains inconsistent results.

paras: It is taken as capsules, tincture or tea in the evening, often alongside other calming herbs. People judge it by sleep over a couple of weeks.

Reported effects include headache and diarrhea. It can add to the sedation of alcohol and other sedatives, and pregnancy use is discouraged. A 1998 report described delirium and cardiac complications on withdrawal.

angle.text: Valerian root is a traditional herbal sleep aid used in bedtime and calming routines, with better sleep seen as supporting skin, recovery and looks. Trial results for sleep are mixed; appearance outcomes have not been studied.

lead: Valerian is a perennial plant (Valeriana officinalis) native to Europe and Asia whose dried root and rhizome are a traditional herbal remedy and a common over-the-counter supplement, mainly for sleep and nervous tension [1][2]. In looksmaxxing and recovery communities it appears in bedtime and anxiety-calming routines, on the reasoning that deeper sleep supports recovery, skin, and a rested look.

Research on its effect on sleep is mixed. Wikipedia summarizes a 2010 meta-analysis and a 2006 systematic review as suggesting possible benefit, while a 2015 systematic review and a 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline described effectiveness as weak or inconclusive; a 2020 meta-analysis concluded it may be safe and effective and suggested inconsistent results could reflect variable extract quality [1][3]. A 2006 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for anxiety disorders [1].

The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) states that valerian is generally safe for short-term use by most adults, that evidence for sleep is inconsistent, and that long-term safety is unknown [2]. Wikipedia and the research literature describe variation in extract quality as one reason results differ between trials [1][3].
infobox: EMA recognizes a dry root extract as a well-established herbal medicine; US: generally recognized as safe at common doses

paras: Valerian is most commonly taken as capsules, tinctures, teas or standardized extracts before bed, and sometimes combined with other herbs such as lavender, hops, passionflower or lemon balm [1][4]. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of 60 studies (6,894 participants) looked at sleep problems and associated disorders, with meta-analyses of subjective sleep quality in 10 studies and anxiety in 8 studies; the authors proposed that inconsistent outcomes were possibly due to variable extract quality, that whole root or rhizome preparations might give more reliable effects, and that combinations with other herbs could improve benefit [3].

NCCIH reports that valerian was historically used for insomnia, migraine, fatigue and stomach cramps, and today is promoted for insomnia, anxiety, stress and depression [2]. Some small studies suggest possible benefit for menopausal symptoms, which NCCIH describes as not conclusive [2]. Registered trials examine it in menopausal women with insomnia [5].

The root contains a volatile oil with sesquiterpenes such as valerenic acid, along with iridoids (valepotriates), alkaloids and flavonoids [1]. Laboratory work found a binding site on GABA-A receptors for valerenic acid and valerenol, where they enhanced the response to GABA [6]. Rat experiments reported anxiolytic behavior with root extracts [7], and zebrafish studies reported delayed seizure onset [8]. These are preclinical findings.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial found that a valerian extract altered functional brain connectivity in healthy participants [9]. A 2014 review of valerian's interaction potential found no evidence for clinically relevant interactions with other drugs [10].

A 1982 study of 128 people comparing an aqueous valerian extract with placebo and a commercial preparation reported a significant decrease in subjectively rated sleep latency [11]. Other early human studies include a 1985 paper on valerian and human sleep [12] and a 1989 double-blind study [13]. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis examined valerian for sleep problems and related disorders [14]. Registered trials have tested valerian in older adults, people with Parkinson's disease, menopausal women, combinations with lavender or poppy extracts, and dental anxiety [15][16][4][5][17].

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline recommends against its use for chronic insomnia in adults, according to NCCIH, which also says evidence for anxiety, depression, stress and menstrual symptoms is insufficient [2]. Wikipedia, by contrast, notes that a 2010 meta-analysis and a 2006 systematic review suggested possible benefit for sleep [1]. A 2006 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for anxiety disorders [1].

Headache and diarrhea occurred in clinical studies, and use is discouraged in pregnancy; as it can depress the central nervous system, it should not be combined with alcohol, benzodiazepines or other sedatives [1]. A 1998 JAMA report described cardiac complications and delirium associated with valerian withdrawal [18]. Product concentration and contaminants vary because supplements are loosely regulated [1]. A US drug label for a valerian, passionflower and magnesium carbonate product advises pregnant or nursing people to seek professional advice [19].

NCCIH lists headache, stomach upset, mental dullness, excitability, uneasiness and vivid dreams as possible side effects, notes that stopping abruptly after long-term use may cause withdrawal-type symptoms such as anxiety, irritability and insomnia, and says liver injury has been reported in very rare cases, mostly with combination herbal products [2]. Little is known about safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding [2]. The 2020 meta-analysis reported no severe adverse events in participants aged 7 to 80 [3].
Valerian has been used since ancient Greece and Rome; Hippocrates described its properties and Galen prescribed it for insomnia [1].

The name valerian is associated with the Latin valere, to be strong or healthy, and the plant was long used across Europe before becoming a mainstream over-the-counter sleep supplement [1]. A European regulator recognises a dry root extract as a well-established herbal medicine, while in the US it is sold as a dietary supplement [1].

Valerian is sold in many forms, from single-herb capsules to multi-ingredient bedtime blends; the US drug label for one valerian, passionflower and magnesium carbonate product advises pregnant or nursing people to seek professional advice [19]. A 2003 JAMA analysis of internet marketing of herbal products examined how herbal supplements are promoted online [20]. In forum supplement stacks, valerian species appear in blended cognitive formulas alongside herbs such as bacopa and ashwagandha [21].
